shortQuestions: Everyday speeds (cars, trains at 20–40 m/s) would then be close to the speed of light, so relativistic effects would be obvious.
Moving vehicles would look shorter (length contraction), clocks in them would run slow (time dilation) and their mass would increase; nothing could move faster than 50 m/s.
We would also see events noticeably late, and moving objects would show strong Doppler colour changes.
By Wien's displacement law λ_max T = constant (2.9 × 10⁻³ m K).
Blue stars emit most strongly at shorter wavelengths, so they have the higher surface temperature; reddish stars are cooler.
No. Photoemission occurs only if the photon energy hf is greater than the work function of the metal.
Different metals have different work functions (threshold frequencies), so light that ejects electrons from one metal (e.g. zinc in UV) may not eject any from another (e.g. platinum).
No. By Wien's law a filament at 2500 K has λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/2500 ≈ 1.2 μm, in the infrared; most of its radiation is infrared and its visible light is yellowish-red.
The Sun at 6000 K has λ_max ≈ 480 nm, in the middle of the visible spectrum, so its light is much whiter.
Energy of one photon E = hc/λ. Red light has a longer wavelength, so each red photon carries less energy.
For the same total energy, the red beam contains the greater number of photons.
A photon always travels at the speed of light c.
Relativistic mass m = m₀/√(1 − v²/c²) would be infinite at v = c unless the rest mass m₀ = 0.
So the rest mass of a photon must be zero; its energy is entirely kinetic, E = pc = hf.
The maximum Compton shift is 2h/(m_ec) ≈ 4.9 × 10⁻¹² m.
Visible light has λ ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁷ m, so the fractional change (≈ 10⁻⁵) is far too small to detect.
Moreover, visible photons (≈ 2–3 eV) are comparable to electron binding energies, so the electrons do not behave as free particles; Compton scattering is noticeable only for X-rays and γ-rays.
Same de Broglie wavelength means the same momentum: m_ev_e = m_pv_p.
The electron has much smaller mass, so it has the greater speed (about 1836 times that of the proton).
Both gain the same kinetic energy K = eV.
λ = h/p = h/√(2mK). The electron has much smaller mass, so smaller momentum.
Hence the electron has the longer de Broglie wavelength.
Ultraviolet photons have higher frequency and energy (about 3–12 eV) than visible photons (about 1.8–3 eV).
UV photons can break chemical bonds and ionise molecules, damaging the DNA and proteins in skin cells — causing sunburn, ageing and skin cancer. Visible photons do not carry enough energy to do this.
longQuestions: A frame of reference is a coordinate system with respect to which positions and motions are measured.

Inertial frame: a frame that is at rest or moves with uniform velocity (not accelerated); Newton's laws hold in it. Examples: a train moving smoothly at constant velocity, the Earth for most everyday purposes, a spacecraft drifting freely.

Non-inertial frame: an accelerated (or rotating) frame; Newton's laws do not hold without introducing fictitious forces. Examples: a car braking or turning (passengers are thrown forward or outward), a lift accelerating upward, a merry-go-round.
Special relativity deals with inertial frames; all inertial frames are equivalent.
Postulate 1 (principle of relativity): the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.
Postulate 2: the speed of light in vacuum is the same (c) for all inertial observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.
Results: (i) Time dilation — a moving clock runs slow: t = t₀/√(1 − v²/c²). (ii) Length contraction — a moving length shrinks along the motion: L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²).
(iii) Mass increase: m = m₀/√(1 − v²/c²). (iv) Mass–energy equivalence: E = mc²; rest energy m₀c². (v) Relativity of simultaneity; no material body can reach the speed of light.
These results are confirmed by muon decay, particle accelerators and GPS clocks.
A black body absorbs all radiation falling on it and is also the best emitter. Its radiation depends only on its temperature.

Features: the intensity–wavelength curve is continuous with a peak; the peak shifts to shorter wavelengths as temperature rises (Wien's law λ_maxT = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K); the total energy radiated per second per unit area rises as T⁴ (Stefan's law E = σT⁴).
Classical theory (Rayleigh–Jeans) predicted infinite energy at short wavelengths — the 'ultraviolet catastrophe'.
Planck's quantum theory: energy is emitted or absorbed not continuously but in discrete packets (quanta) of energy E = hf, h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. His formula fitted the experimental curves exactly.
Importance: it began quantum physics — leading to Einstein's photon theory, Bohr's atom and quantum mechanics.
Photoelectric effect: emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency falls on it.

Observations: no emission below a threshold frequency, however intense the light; the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends on frequency, not intensity; the number of electrons (current) depends on intensity; emission is instantaneous.
Failure of classical (wave) theory: it predicted emission at any frequency with enough intensity, K.E. increasing with intensity, and a time delay at low intensity — all contrary to experiment.
Photon explanation (Einstein): light consists of photons of energy hf. One photon gives all its energy to one electron: hf = φ + K_max, where φ = hf₀ is the work function.
This explains the threshold frequency (hf < φ gives no emission), K_max increasing linearly with f, current ∝ number of photons (intensity), and instant emission.
Compton effect: when X-rays are scattered by loosely bound (free) electrons, the scattered X-rays have a longer wavelength than the incident ones, depending on the scattering angle.
Treat the X-ray as a photon of energy hf and momentum h/λ colliding elastically with an electron at rest.
Energy conservation: hc/λ + m₀c² = hc/λ′ + mc². Momentum conservation along and perpendicular to the incident direction: h/λ = (h/λ′) cos θ + p cos φ; 0 = (h/λ′) sin θ − p sin φ.
Eliminating the electron's recoil angle φ and momentum p (using E² = p²c² + m₀²c⁴) gives:
Δλ = λ′ − λ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ). h/m₀c = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m is the Compton wavelength. Δλ is zero at θ = 0 and maximum (2h/m₀c) at θ = 180°. This confirmed the particle (photon) nature of light.
Pair production: a high-energy γ-ray photon passing near a heavy nucleus disappears and an electron–positron pair is created: γ → e⁻ + e⁺.
Minimum photon energy = 2m₀c² = 1.02 MeV; any extra energy becomes the kinetic energy of the pair: hf = 2m₀c² + K₋ + K₊. The nucleus is needed to conserve momentum; charge is conserved (−e + e = 0).
Annihilation: when a positron meets an electron, both disappear and their mass is converted into energy — usually two γ-photons of 0.51 MeV each, moving in opposite directions (to conserve momentum).
These processes show the conversion of energy into matter and matter into energy, confirming E = mc². Annihilation is used in PET scanning.
De Broglie hypothesis: just as light has particle properties, moving material particles have wave properties. The wavelength of a particle of momentum p is λ = h/p = h/(mv).
Davisson–Germer experiment (or G. P. Thomson's): a beam of electrons accelerated through a known p.d. was directed at a nickel crystal (or a thin metal foil).
The scattered electrons showed intensity maxima at particular angles — a diffraction pattern, like X-rays diffracted by a crystal (or rings like light through a fine grating).
The wavelength found from the diffraction (Bragg's law) agreed with λ = h/p calculated from the accelerating voltage (e.g. 54 V gives 0.167 nm).
Diffraction is a wave property, so this proved that electrons have wave nature. It is the basis of the electron microscope.
Wave–particle duality: both light and matter show wave properties in some experiments and particle properties in others.
Light: interference, diffraction and polarisation show wave nature; the photoelectric effect, Compton effect and pair production show particle (photon) nature.
Matter: electrons, neutrons and atoms behave as particles (definite mass, charge, collisions) but also diffract like waves (Davisson–Germer), with λ = h/p.
The two aspects never appear together in one experiment; which one is seen depends on the experiment (Bohr's principle of complementarity). The link is E = hf and p = h/λ.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: it is impossible to measure simultaneously both the position and the momentum of a particle with unlimited accuracy: Δx Δp ≥ h/(4π). Similarly ΔE Δt ≥ h/(4π).
It is not due to imperfect instruments; it is a fundamental consequence of the wave nature of matter.
Thought experiment (gamma-ray microscope): to locate an electron we must illuminate it. The position uncertainty is about the wavelength used: Δx ≈ λ.
The photon that reveals the electron gives it a recoil momentum of about h/λ, which is unknown: Δp ≈ h/λ.
So Δx Δp ≈ h. Using shorter λ improves Δx but increases Δp, and vice versa — the product can never be reduced below the order of h.
